NUS ST5227 — Applied Statistical Learning¶

Detailed, systematic, intuitive notebook with Bokeh visualisations¶

This notebook treats statistical learning as a connected framework rather than a list of APIs.

For each major idea we ask:

  1. What problem is being solved?
  2. What assumptions are made?
  3. What objective is optimized?
  4. How does the estimator behave?
  5. Where do bias and variance enter?
  6. What controls model complexity?
  7. How do we validate generalization?
  8. How do we interpret the result?

Main topics¶

  • statistical learning and empirical risk;
  • bias–variance trade-off;
  • ordinary least squares and projection geometry;
  • heteroscedasticity and weighted least squares;
  • Ridge and LASSO regularization;
  • cross-validation and model selection;
  • high-dimensional $p>n$ learning;
  • logistic regression, likelihood and Newton–Raphson;
  • polynomial basis expansion and splines;
  • KNN and the curse of dimensionality;
  • decision trees;
  • SVMs and kernels;
  • end-to-end regression and classification case studies;
  • computational and methodological trade-offs.

All visualisations use Bokeh.

1. Setup¶

The examples use only standard scientific Python packages and built-in scikit-learn datasets, so the notebook does not depend on an internet connection.

We use one random seed throughout for reproducibility.

2. Reusable evaluation and Bokeh helpers¶

Repeated experiment code is a common source of inconsistencies.

We centralize:

  • metric calculations;
  • table display;
  • reusable scatter plots;
  • two-dimensional probability surfaces.

This is also a useful software-engineering habit: isolate evaluation and visualisation from model training.

In [39]:
@dataclass
class RegressionMetrics:
    rmse: float
    mae: float
    r2: float

@dataclass
class ClassificationMetrics:
    accuracy: float
    balanced_accuracy: float
    f1: float
    roc_auc: float

class Evaluator:
    @staticmethod
    def regression(y_true, y_pred):
        return RegressionMetrics(
            rmse=float(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred) ** 0.5),
            mae=float(mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred)),
            r2=float(r2_score(y_true, y_pred)),
        )

    @staticmethod
    def classification(y_true, y_pred, y_prob=None):
        auc = np.nan if y_prob is None else roc_auc_score(y_true, y_prob)
        return ClassificationMetrics(
            accuracy=float(accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred)),
            balanced_accuracy=float(balanced_accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred)),
            f1=float(f1_score(y_true, y_pred)),
            roc_auc=float(auc),
        )

def show_df_table(df, title, width=900, height=260):
    x = df.copy().reset_index(drop=True)
    x.columns = [str(c) for c in x.columns]
    src = ColumnDataSource(x)

    columns = []
    for c in x.columns:
        if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(x[c]):
            columns.append(TableColumn(
                field=c, title=c.replace("_", " ").title(),
                formatter=NumberFormatter(format="0.0000")
            ))
        else:
            columns.append(TableColumn(field=c, title=c.replace("_", " ").title()))

    table = DataTable(
        source=src, columns=columns,
        width=width, height=height,
        index_position=None
    )
    header = figure(
        title=title, width=width, height=45,
        toolbar_location=None, x_range=(0, 1), y_range=(0, 1)
    )
    header.axis.visible = False
    header.grid.visible = False
    show(column(header, table))

def scatter_plot(x, y, title, x_label, y_label, width=820, height=460):
    p = figure(
        title=title, width=width, height=height,
        x_axis_label=x_label, y_axis_label=y_label,
        tools="pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset,save,hover"
    )
    p.scatter(x, y, size=7, alpha=0.65)
    return p

def decision_surface(model, X, y, title, grid_size=160, width=760, height=540):
    X = np.asarray(X)
    y = np.asarray(y)

    x_min, x_max = X[:, 0].min() - 1, X[:, 0].max() + 1
    y_min, y_max = X[:, 1].min() - 1, X[:, 1].max() + 1

    xx = np.linspace(x_min, x_max, grid_size)
    yy = np.linspace(y_min, y_max, grid_size)
    gx, gy = np.meshgrid(xx, yy)
    grid = np.column_stack([gx.ravel(), gy.ravel()])

    if hasattr(model, "predict_proba"):
        z = model.predict_proba(grid)
        z = z[:, 1] if z.ndim == 2 else z
    else:
        z = expit(model.decision_function(grid))

    z = z.reshape(gx.shape)

    p = figure(
        title=title, width=width, height=height,
        x_axis_label="feature 1", y_axis_label="feature 2",
        tools="pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset,save,hover"
    )
    p.image(
        image=[z], x=x_min, y=y_min,
        dw=x_max-x_min, dh=y_max-y_min,
        palette="Viridis256", alpha=0.35
    )

    for cls in np.unique(y):
        mask = y == cls
        p.scatter(
            X[mask, 0], X[mask, 1],
            size=7, alpha=0.70,
            legend_label=f"class {cls}"
        )
    p.legend.location = "top_left"
    return p

3. The core statistical-learning problem¶

Assume

$$ Y=f(X)+\epsilon, $$

where:

  • $f(X)$ is systematic signal;
  • $\epsilon$ is irreducible noise.

Given a finite training sample

$$ \mathcal D=\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n, $$

we estimate $f$ with $\hat f$.

The key difficulty is that we never observe the true $f$ directly in real problems.

In [34]:
def true_function(x):
    return 2.0 + 1.5*x - 0.8*x**2 + 0.12*x**3

n = 120
x = rng.uniform(-4, 4, size=n)
y = true_function(x) + rng.normal(0, 3.0, size=n)
x_grid = np.linspace(-4, 4, 400)

p = scatter_plot(
    x, y,
    "Observed sample versus the hidden data-generating function",
    "x", "y"
)
p.line(x_grid, true_function(x_grid), line_width=4, legend_label="true f(x)")
p.legend.location = "top_left"
show(p)

What should you notice?¶

The observed data are noisy realizations around an underlying curve.

A learner must distinguish:

$$ \text{signal} \quad\text{from}\quad \text{noise}. $$

If a model is too rigid, it misses real structure.

If it is too flexible, it may model accidental noise.

That is the motivation for the bias–variance trade-off.

4. Bias–variance trade-off¶

For squared-error prediction, expected prediction error can be decomposed as

$$ E[(Y_0-\hat f(x_0))^2] = \sigma^2 + \operatorname{Bias}[\hat f(x_0)]^2 + \operatorname{Var}[\hat f(x_0)]. $$

  • $\sigma^2$: irreducible noise;
  • Bias$^2$: error caused by systematic misspecification;
  • Variance: sensitivity to the sampled training set.

A useful way to see this is to vary polynomial degree.

In [38]:
X = x.reshape(-1, 1)
degrees = [1, 3, 8, 15]

p = scatter_plot(
    x, y,
    "Polynomial complexity: underfitting to overfitting",
    "x", "y",
    width=900, height=500
)

for degree in degrees:
    model = Pipeline([
        ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=degree, include_bias=False)),
        ("reg", LinearRegression())
    ])
    model.fit(X, y)
    pred = model.predict(x_grid.reshape(-1, 1))
    p.line(x_grid, pred, line_width=2, legend_label=f"degree {degree}")

p.line(
    x_grid, true_function(x_grid),
    line_width=4, line_dash="dashed",
    legend_label="true function"
)
p.legend.location = "top_left"
p.legend.click_policy = "hide"
show(p)

Interpretation¶

A low-degree model tends to have:

$$ \text{high bias},\qquad \text{low variance}. $$

A very high-degree model tends toward:

$$ \text{lower training bias},\qquad \text{higher variance}. $$

The goal is therefore not to minimize training error blindly.

The goal is to find a level of flexibility that produces low out-of-sample risk.

5. Empirical risk versus population risk¶

A model $f_\theta$ is usually fitted by minimizing a sample-based objective:

$$ \hat R(\theta) = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^{n} L(y_i,f_\theta(x_i)). $$

For squared-error regression,

$$ L(y,\hat y)=(y-\hat y)^2. $$

But the true quantity of interest is

$$ R(\theta) = E[L(Y,f_\theta(X))]. $$

We do not know the population distribution, so we cannot calculate $R(\theta)$ directly.

Cross-validation later acts as an estimator of generalization performance.

6. Ordinary Least Squares¶

For multiple regression,

$$ Y=X\beta+\epsilon. $$

OLS minimizes

$$ RSS(\beta) = (Y-X\beta)^T(Y-X\beta). $$

Differentiating,

$$ \nabla RSS(\beta) = -2X^TY+2X^TX\beta. $$

Set the gradient to zero:

$$ X^TX\hat\beta=X^TY. $$

When $X^TX$ is invertible,

$$ \boxed{ \hat\beta=(X^TX)^{-1}X^TY }. $$

In numerical code, solving a linear system is preferable to explicitly forming the inverse.

In [37]:
X_demo = np.column_stack([
    np.ones(n), x, x**2, x**3
])

beta_closed = np.linalg.solve(X_demo.T @ X_demo, X_demo.T @ y)

sk = LinearRegression().fit(X_demo[:, 1:], y)
beta_sklearn = np.r_[sk.intercept_, sk.coef_]

coef_compare = pd.DataFrame({
    "term": ["intercept", "x", "x^2", "x^3"],
    "closed_form": beta_closed,
    "sklearn": beta_sklearn,
    "abs_difference": np.abs(beta_closed-beta_sklearn)
})

show_df_table(coef_compare, "Closed-form OLS versus scikit-learn")

WARNING:bokeh.core.validation.check:W-1000 (MISSING_RENDERERS): Plot has no renderers: figure(id='p3486', ...)

Statistical behavior of OLS¶

Write

$$ \hat\beta = \beta+(X^TX)^{-1}X^T\epsilon. $$

If

$$ E[\epsilon]=0, $$

then

$$ E[\hat\beta]=\beta. $$

So OLS is unbiased.

Under homoscedastic errors,

$$ \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)=\sigma^2I, $$

we obtain

$$ \boxed{ \operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta) = \sigma^2(X^TX)^{-1}. } $$

This formula explains why near-collinear predictors can make coefficient estimates unstable.

7. OLS as a geometric projection¶

The fitted values are

$$ \hat Y=X\hat\beta. $$

Define

$$ H=X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T. $$

Then

$$ \hat Y=HY. $$

$H$ is the hat matrix.

It is an orthogonal projection matrix because

$$ H^T=H $$

and

$$ H^2=H. $$

The residual vector

$$ e=Y-\hat Y $$

satisfies

$$ X^Te=0. $$

So the residual is orthogonal to every direction in the predictor space.

In [36]:
H = X_demo @ np.linalg.solve(X_demo.T @ X_demo, X_demo.T)
y_hat = H @ y
resid = y - y_hat

projection_checks = pd.DataFrame({
    "property": [
        "norm(X^T e)",
        "trace(H)",
        "norm(H^2-H)",
        "norm(H^T-H)"
    ],
    "value": [
        np.linalg.norm(X_demo.T @ resid),
        np.trace(H),
        np.linalg.norm(H @ H - H),
        np.linalg.norm(H.T - H)
    ]
})

show_df_table(projection_checks, "Numerical projection checks")

8. Multicollinearity¶

Suppose two predictors are nearly duplicates:

$$ X_2\approx X_1. $$

Then the model can estimate their combined effect reasonably well while being uncertain about how to divide that effect between $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$.

The matrix $X^TX$ becomes ill-conditioned.

Since

$$ \operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta)=\sigma^2(X^TX)^{-1}, $$

small eigenvalues of $X^TX$ lead to large estimator variance.

In [41]:
n_mc = 250
x1 = rng.normal(size=n_mc)
x2 = x1 + rng.normal(scale=0.03, size=n_mc)
y_mc = 4 + 3*x1 + 3*x2 + rng.normal(scale=1.0, size=n_mc)

X_mc = np.column_stack([x1, x2])
ols_mc = LinearRegression().fit(X_mc, y_mc)

mc_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "quantity": ["coef x1", "coef x2", "condition number of X^T X"],
    "value": [
        ols_mc.coef_[0],
        ols_mc.coef_[1],
        np.linalg.cond(X_mc.T @ X_mc)
    ]
})

show_df_table(mc_summary, "Multicollinearity diagnostics")

9. Heteroscedasticity and Weighted Least Squares¶

OLS assumes constant error variance:

$$ \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_i|X_i)=\sigma^2. $$

If instead

$$ \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_i|X_i)=\sigma_i^2, $$

then observations have different reliability.

Weighted Least Squares solves

$$ \min_\beta (Y-X\beta)^TW(Y-X\beta), $$

typically with

$$ w_i\propto\frac{1}{\sigma_i^2}. $$

The solution is

$$ \boxed{ \hat\beta_{WLS} = (X^TWX)^{-1}X^TWY. } $$

In [40]:
n_w = 350
x_w = rng.uniform(0.2, 8.0, size=n_w)
sigma_w = 0.4 + 0.55*x_w
y_w = 2.0 + 1.8*x_w + rng.normal(scale=sigma_w)

X_w = np.column_stack([np.ones(n_w), x_w])

beta_ols = np.linalg.solve(X_w.T @ X_w, X_w.T @ y_w)

weights = 1/sigma_w**2
WX = X_w * weights[:, None]
beta_wls = np.linalg.solve(X_w.T @ WX, X_w.T @ (weights*y_w))

g = np.linspace(x_w.min(), x_w.max(), 250)

p = scatter_plot(
    x_w, y_w,
    "Heteroscedastic data: OLS versus WLS",
    "x", "y",
    width=900, height=500
)
p.line(g, beta_ols[0]+beta_ols[1]*g, line_width=3, legend_label="OLS")
p.line(g, beta_wls[0]+beta_wls[1]*g, line_width=3, legend_label="WLS")
p.line(g, 2.0+1.8*g, line_width=3, line_dash="dashed", legend_label="true relation")
p.legend.location = "top_left"
show(p)

WLS intuition¶

WLS deliberately makes noisy observations less influential.

An equivalent viewpoint is to premultiply the problem by $W^{1/2}$:

$$ W^{1/2}Y = W^{1/2}X\beta + W^{1/2}\epsilon. $$

After transformation, the errors can be closer to equal variance, allowing ordinary least squares machinery to be reused.

10. Ridge regression¶

Ridge augments squared error with an $L_2$ penalty:

$$ \hat\beta_{\text{ridge}} = \arg\min_\beta \left[ \|Y-X\beta\|_2^2 + \lambda\|\beta\|_2^2 \right]. $$

For standardized predictors,

$$ \boxed{ \hat\beta_{\text{ridge}} = (X^TX+\lambda I)^{-1}X^TY. } $$

The important point is that Ridge intentionally introduces bias to reduce variance.

$$ \lambda\uparrow \Rightarrow \text{Bias}\uparrow,\quad \text{Variance}\downarrow. $$

In [9]:
X_mc_s = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_mc)
alphas = np.logspace(-4, 4, 80)

rows = []
for alpha in alphas:
    model = Ridge(alpha=alpha).fit(X_mc_s, y_mc)
    rows.append({
        "alpha": alpha,
        "coef_x1": model.coef_[0],
        "coef_x2": model.coef_[1],
        "coef_norm": np.linalg.norm(model.coef_)
    })

ridge_path = pd.DataFrame(rows)

p = figure(
    title="Ridge coefficient paths",
    width=900, height=460,
    x_axis_type="log",
    x_axis_label="alpha",
    y_axis_label="coefficient",
    tools="pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset,save,hover"
)
p.line(ridge_path["alpha"], ridge_path["coef_x1"], line_width=3, legend_label="x1")
p.line(ridge_path["alpha"], ridge_path["coef_x2"], line_width=3, legend_label="x2")
p.legend.location = "top_right"
show(p)

11. Why Ridge stabilizes small-eigenvalue directions¶

Suppose

$$ X^TX=VDV^T $$

with eigenvalues $d_j$.

OLS effectively uses factors

$$ \frac{1}{d_j}. $$

If $d_j$ is tiny, the inverse explodes.

Ridge changes this to

$$ \frac{1}{d_j+\lambda}. $$

Therefore unstable directions are strongly damped.

In [10]:
XtX = X_mc_s.T @ X_mc_s
eigvals = np.linalg.eigvalsh(XtX)

eigen_df = pd.DataFrame({
    "eigenvalue": eigvals,
    "OLS inverse factor": 1/eigvals,
    "Ridge alpha=1": 1/(eigvals+1),
    "Ridge alpha=10": 1/(eigvals+10)
})

show_df_table(eigen_df, "Ridge damping in eigen-directions")

12. LASSO: regularization plus feature selection¶

LASSO uses an $L_1$ penalty:

$$ \hat\beta_{\text{lasso}} = \arg\min_\beta \left[ \frac{1}{2n}\|Y-X\beta\|_2^2 + \lambda\sum_j|\beta_j| \right]. $$

Unlike Ridge, LASSO can set coefficients exactly to zero.

So LASSO can simultaneously perform:

$$ \boxed{ \text{estimation} + \text{shrinkage} + \text{feature selection}. } $$

In [11]:
X_lasso, y_lasso, coef_true = make_regression(
    n_samples=300,
    n_features=12,
    n_informative=4,
    noise=18,
    coef=True,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE
)
X_lasso = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_lasso)

alphas_lasso = np.logspace(-2.5, 2.0, 70)
rows = []

for alpha in alphas_lasso:
    model = Lasso(alpha=alpha, max_iter=20000).fit(X_lasso, y_lasso)
    rec = {"alpha": alpha, "nonzero": np.sum(np.abs(model.coef_) > 1e-8)}
    for j, c in enumerate(model.coef_):
        rec[f"x{j}"] = c
    rows.append(rec)

lasso_path = pd.DataFrame(rows)

p = figure(
    title="LASSO coefficient paths",
    width=920, height=500,
    x_axis_type="log",
    x_axis_label="alpha",
    y_axis_label="coefficient",
    tools="pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset,save,hover"
)
for j in range(12):
    p.line(lasso_path["alpha"], lasso_path[f"x{j}"], line_width=2, legend_label=f"x{j}")
p.legend.location = "top_right"
p.legend.click_policy = "hide"
show(p)
In [12]:
p = figure(
    title="LASSO sparsity path",
    width=820, height=430,
    x_axis_type="log",
    x_axis_label="alpha",
    y_axis_label="number of non-zero coefficients",
    tools="pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset,save,hover"
)
p.line(lasso_path["alpha"], lasso_path["nonzero"], line_width=3)
p.scatter(lasso_path["alpha"], lasso_path["nonzero"], size=5)
show(p)

Ridge versus LASSO¶

Ridge¶

Useful when many predictors may carry signal, especially when they are correlated.

LASSO¶

Useful when a sparse model is plausible.

The geometry differs:

$$ L_2:\quad \sum_j\beta_j^2 $$

versus

$$ L_1:\quad \sum_j|\beta_j|. $$

The non-smooth corner of the $L_1$ penalty at zero is what allows exact sparsity.

13. Cross-validation and model selection¶

A hyperparameter should not be tuned on the final test set.

For $K$-fold cross-validation:

$$ CV(\lambda) = \frac1K \sum_{k=1}^K L_k(\lambda). $$

Procedure:

  1. divide training data into folds;
  2. train on $K-1$ folds;
  3. evaluate on the remaining fold;
  4. rotate the validation fold;
  5. average the losses;
  6. choose the best hyperparameter;
  7. refit using all training data;
  8. evaluate once on the untouched test set.
In [13]:
X_cv, y_cv = make_regression(
    n_samples=500,
    n_features=30,
    n_informative=10,
    noise=35,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE
)

X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
    X_cv, y_cv, test_size=0.25, random_state=RANDOM_STATE
)

alphas_cv = np.logspace(-4, 4, 60)
kf = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

cv_rows = []
for alpha in alphas_cv:
    model = Pipeline([
        ("scale", StandardScaler()),
        ("ridge", Ridge(alpha=alpha))
    ])
    mse = -cross_val_score(
        model, X_tr, y_tr,
        scoring="neg_mean_squared_error",
        cv=kf, n_jobs=-1
    )
    cv_rows.append({
        "alpha": alpha,
        "cv_mse_mean": mse.mean(),
        "cv_mse_sd": mse.std(ddof=1)
    })

cv_df = pd.DataFrame(cv_rows)
best_alpha = float(cv_df.loc[cv_df["cv_mse_mean"].idxmin(), "alpha"])

p = figure(
    title="Cross-validation curve for Ridge",
    width=900, height=460,
    x_axis_type="log",
    x_axis_label="alpha",
    y_axis_label="mean CV MSE",
    tools="pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset,save,hover"
)
p.line(cv_df["alpha"], cv_df["cv_mse_mean"], line_width=3)
p.scatter(cv_df["alpha"], cv_df["cv_mse_mean"], size=5)
p.add_layout(Span(location=best_alpha, dimension="height", line_dash="dashed", line_width=2))
show(p)

print(f"Selected alpha = {best_alpha:.6g}")

Selected alpha = 2.98247
In [14]:
final_ridge = Pipeline([
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ("ridge", Ridge(alpha=best_alpha))
])
final_ridge.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
pred = final_ridge.predict(X_te)

final_metrics = Evaluator.regression(y_te, pred)
pd.DataFrame([final_metrics.__dict__])

14. High-dimensional learning: $p>n$¶

Suppose

$$ n=80,\qquad p=300. $$

Then $X^TX$ is rank deficient, so the unregularized normal-equation solution is not unique.

Ridge resolves this because

$$ X^TX+\lambda I $$

is invertible for $\lambda>0$.

This is one reason regularization is essential in modern high-dimensional statistics.

In [15]:
X_hd, y_hd = make_regression(
    n_samples=80,
    n_features=300,
    n_informative=12,
    noise=25,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE
)

rank_xtx = np.linalg.matrix_rank(X_hd.T @ X_hd)

ridge_hd = Pipeline([
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ("ridge", Ridge(alpha=10))
]).fit(X_hd, y_hd)

print("n =", X_hd.shape[0])
print("p =", X_hd.shape[1])
print("rank(X^T X) =", rank_xtx)
print("Ridge fit succeeded even though p > n.")

n = 80
p = 300
rank(X^T X) = 80
Ridge fit succeeded even though p > n.

15. Logistic regression as a GLM¶

For binary outcomes,

$$ Y\in\{0,1\}. $$

Let

$$ p(x)=P(Y=1|X=x). $$

The logit link is

$$ \log\frac{p(x)}{1-p(x)} = \beta_0+x^T\beta. $$

Therefore

$$ \boxed{ p(x)= \frac{1}{1+\exp[-(\beta_0+x^T\beta)]}. } $$

The sigmoid transforms any real-valued score into a valid probability.

In [42]:
z = np.linspace(-8, 8, 400)

p = figure(
    title="Logistic sigmoid",
    width=820, height=430,
    x_axis_label="linear predictor z",
    y_axis_label="probability",
    tools="pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset,save,hover"
)
p.line(z, expit(z), line_width=4)
p.add_layout(Span(location=0.5, dimension="width", line_dash="dashed"))
p.add_layout(Span(location=0, dimension="height", line_dash="dotted"))
show(p)

16. Logistic regression as maximum likelihood¶

For one Bernoulli observation,

$$ P(Y_i=y_i) = p_i^{y_i}(1-p_i)^{1-y_i}. $$

The likelihood is

$$ L(\beta) = \prod_i p_i^{y_i}(1-p_i)^{1-y_i}. $$

Its log is

$$ \ell(\beta) = \sum_i [ y_i\log p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i) ]. $$

Maximizing $\ell(\beta)$ is equivalent to minimizing negative log-likelihood.

That negative log-likelihood is the familiar binary cross-entropy used in machine learning.

So:

$$ \boxed{ \text{statistical maximum likelihood} = \text{machine-learning loss minimization}. } $$

17. Newton–Raphson optimization¶

OLS has a closed-form solution; logistic regression generally does not.

Newton's method updates

$$ \beta_{t+1} = \beta_t - H(\beta_t)^{-1}\nabla f(\beta_t). $$

For negative logistic log-likelihood:

$$ \nabla f(\beta)=X^T(p-y) $$

and

$$ H(\beta)=X^TWX, $$

where

$$ W_{ii}=p_i(1-p_i). $$

We implement a small solver to expose the optimization mechanics.

In [43]:
class NewtonLogisticRegression:
    def __init__(self, max_iter=50, tol=1e-8, l2=1e-6):
        self.max_iter = max_iter
        self.tol = tol
        self.l2 = l2
        self.coef_ = None
        self.history_ = []

    @staticmethod
    def _with_intercept(X):
        return np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X)), X])

    def fit(self, X, y):
        Xb = self._with_intercept(np.asarray(X))
        y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)

        beta = np.zeros(Xb.shape[1])
        I = np.eye(Xb.shape[1])
        I[0, 0] = 0

        for iteration in range(self.max_iter):
            p = expit(Xb @ beta)
            eps = 1e-12

            nll = -np.sum(
                y*np.log(p+eps) + (1-y)*np.log(1-p+eps)
            ) + 0.5*self.l2*np.sum(beta[1:]**2)

            grad = Xb.T @ (p-y) + self.l2*(I @ beta)
            w = p*(1-p)
            H = Xb.T @ (Xb*w[:, None]) + self.l2*I

            step = np.linalg.solve(H, grad)
            beta_new = beta - step

            self.history_.append({
                "iteration": iteration,
                "nll": nll,
                "step_norm": np.linalg.norm(step)
            })

            if np.linalg.norm(beta_new-beta) < self.tol:
                beta = beta_new
                break

            beta = beta_new

        self.coef_ = beta
        return self

    def predict_proba(self, X):
        return expit(self._with_intercept(np.asarray(X)) @ self.coef_)

    def predict(self, X, threshold=0.5):
        return (self.predict_proba(X) >= threshold).astype(int)
In [44]:
X_cls, y_cls = make_classification(
    n_samples=500,
    n_features=2,
    n_redundant=0,
    n_informative=2,
    n_clusters_per_class=1,
    class_sep=1.4,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE
)

X_cls_s = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_cls)

newton_model = NewtonLogisticRegression().fit(X_cls_s, y_cls)
hist = pd.DataFrame(newton_model.history_)

p = figure(
    title="Newton–Raphson convergence",
    width=820, height=430,
    x_axis_label="iteration",
    y_axis_label="negative log-likelihood",
    tools="pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset,save,hover"
)
p.line(hist["iteration"], hist["nll"], line_width=3)
p.scatter(hist["iteration"], hist["nll"], size=7)
show(p)
In [19]:
show(
    decision_surface(
        newton_model,
        X_cls_s,
        y_cls,
        "Logistic regression probability surface"
    )
)

Optimization insight¶

Newton–Raphson uses both:

  • the gradient: direction of steepest local change;
  • the Hessian: local curvature.

This often converges quickly near the optimum, but Hessian calculations become costly in very high dimensions.

Large-scale systems may therefore use:

  • gradient descent;
  • stochastic gradient descent;
  • L-BFGS;
  • coordinate descent.

18. Decision thresholds¶

A probabilistic classifier might estimate

$$ P(Y=1|x)=0.37. $$

Classification requires an additional decision rule.

At threshold $t$:

$$ \hat y= \mathbf 1[p(x)\ge t]. $$

Changing $t$ trades false positives against false negatives.

This distinction is crucial:

$$ \boxed{ \text{probability estimation} \neq \text{decision policy}. } $$

In [45]:
probs = newton_model.predict_proba(X_cls_s)
thresholds = np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 19)

rows = []
for t in thresholds:
    pred = (probs >= t).astype(int)
    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_cls, pred).ravel()
    rows.append({
        "threshold": t,
        "accuracy": accuracy_score(y_cls, pred),
        "false_positive_rate": fp/(fp+tn),
        "false_negative_rate": fn/(fn+tp)
    })

thr_df = pd.DataFrame(rows)

p = figure(
    title="Classification threshold trade-offs",
    width=900, height=460,
    x_axis_label="threshold",
    y_axis_label="rate",
    tools="pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset,save,hover"
)
p.line(thr_df["threshold"], thr_df["accuracy"], line_width=3, legend_label="accuracy")
p.line(thr_df["threshold"], thr_df["false_positive_rate"], line_width=3, legend_label="false positive rate")
p.line(thr_df["threshold"], thr_df["false_negative_rate"], line_width=3, legend_label="false negative rate")
p.legend.location = "top_center"
show(p)

19. Basis expansion and polynomial regression¶

A nonlinear function can be represented using basis functions:

$$ f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{K}\beta_jh_j(x). $$

For polynomial regression:

$$ h_1(x)=x,\quad h_2(x)=x^2,\quad h_3(x)=x^3,\dots $$

The relationship is nonlinear in $x$ but still linear in the coefficients $\beta_j$.

That allows ordinary linear-model machinery to fit nonlinear curves.

In [46]:
degrees = [1, 2, 3, 6, 12]

p = scatter_plot(
    x, y,
    "Polynomial basis expansion",
    "x", "y",
    width=900, height=500
)

for degree in degrees:
    model = Pipeline([
        ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=degree, include_bias=False)),
        ("reg", LinearRegression())
    ]).fit(X, y)

    p.line(
        x_grid,
        model.predict(x_grid.reshape(-1, 1)),
        line_width=2,
        legend_label=f"degree {degree}"
    )

p.legend.location = "top_left"
p.legend.click_policy = "hide"
show(p)

20. Splines¶

High-degree global polynomials can oscillate badly.

Splines construct piecewise low-degree polynomials joined smoothly at knots.

This gives:

  • local flexibility;
  • smooth transitions;
  • better numerical behavior;
  • interpretable complexity control via number and placement of knots.

A smoothing-spline formulation is

$$ \min_f \left[ \sum_i(y_i-f(x_i))^2 + \lambda\int[f''(t)]^2dt \right]. $$

The two terms express the same central tension:

$$ \text{fit} + \lambda\times\text{roughness penalty}. $$

In [47]:
spline_settings = {
    "4 knots": 4,
    "7 knots": 7,
    "12 knots": 12
}

p = scatter_plot(
    x, y,
    "Spline basis complexity",
    "x", "y",
    width=900, height=500
)

for label, knots in spline_settings.items():
    model = Pipeline([
        ("spline", SplineTransformer(
            n_knots=knots,
            degree=3,
            include_bias=False
        )),
        ("ridge", Ridge(alpha=1e-6))
    ]).fit(X, y)

    p.line(
        x_grid,
        model.predict(x_grid.reshape(-1, 1)),
        line_width=3,
        legend_label=label
    )

p.line(
    x_grid, true_function(x_grid),
    line_width=4,
    line_dash="dashed",
    legend_label="true function"
)

p.legend.location = "top_left"
show(p)

21. K-Nearest Neighbours¶

KNN regression estimates

$$ \hat f(x_0) = \frac1K \sum_{i\in N_K(x_0)}y_i. $$

$K$ acts as a smoothing parameter.

Small $K$¶

  • very local;
  • low bias;
  • high variance.

Large $K$¶

  • smoother;
  • higher bias;
  • lower variance.

Thus KNN gives another concrete view of bias–variance trade-off.

In [48]:
k_values = [1, 5, 15, 40]

p = scatter_plot(
    x, y,
    "KNN regression: effect of K",
    "x", "y",
    width=900, height=500
)

for k in k_values:
    model = KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=k).fit(X, y)
    p.line(
        x_grid,
        model.predict(x_grid.reshape(-1, 1)),
        line_width=2,
        legend_label=f"K={k}"
    )

p.legend.location = "top_left"
show(p)

22. Curse of dimensionality¶

KNN relies on nearby observations.

In high dimensions, data become sparse.

Suppose we want a centered hypercube containing fraction $r$ of the unit-hypercube volume.

Its side length must be

$$ r^{1/p}. $$

As $p$ increases, this side length approaches 1.

So a neighborhood containing even a modest fraction of data must span a large proportion of every coordinate range.

The idea of "local" becomes increasingly weak.

In [49]:
dims = np.arange(1, 101)
r = 0.10
side = r**(1/dims)

p = figure(
    title="Curse of dimensionality: side length needed for 10% volume",
    width=880, height=440,
    x_axis_label="dimension p",
    y_axis_label="required side length",
    tools="pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset,save,hover"
)
p.line(dims, side, line_width=3)
show(p)

23. Decision trees¶

Trees recursively partition predictor space.

For regression, a split $X_j<s$ may be selected to minimize within-region squared errors.

For classification, common impurity measures include

$$ Gini=1-\sum_kp_k^2 $$

and

$$ Entropy=-\sum_kp_k\log p_k. $$

A deep tree can create many tiny regions and therefore has high flexibility.

That usually means:

  • lower training error;
  • higher variance;
  • greater overfitting risk.
In [50]:
X_tree, y_tree = make_classification(
    n_samples=600,
    n_features=2,
    n_redundant=0,
    n_informative=2,
    n_clusters_per_class=2,
    class_sep=1.0,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE
)

for depth in [1, 3, 8]:
    tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(
        max_depth=depth,
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE
    ).fit(X_tree, y_tree)

    show(
        decision_surface(
            tree, X_tree, y_tree,
            f"Decision tree: max_depth={depth}"
        )
    )

Tree regularization¶

Common controls include:

  • max_depth;
  • min_samples_leaf;
  • min_samples_split;
  • cost-complexity pruning.

Increasing depth usually increases flexibility.

Increasing minimum leaf size usually decreases flexibility.

Again, the algorithm-specific parameters are different, but the statistical objective is the same:

$$ \boxed{\text{control model complexity}.} $$

24. Support Vector Machines¶

For labels

$$ y_i\in\{-1,+1\}, $$

a linear classifier uses

$$ f(x)=w^Tx+b. $$

SVM seeks a large-margin separator.

The soft-margin objective can be written as

$$ \frac12\|w\|_2^2 + C\sum_i\max(0,1-y_if(x_i)). $$

The first term encourages a wide margin.

The second penalizes margin violations through hinge loss.

So SVM also has the familiar structure:

$$ \boxed{ \text{loss} + \text{regularization}. } $$

In [51]:
X_svm, y_svm = make_classification(
    n_samples=450,
    n_features=2,
    n_redundant=0,
    n_informative=2,
    n_clusters_per_class=1,
    class_sep=1.25,
    random_state=7
)

X_svm_s = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_svm)

svm_linear = SVC(
    kernel="linear",
    C=1.0,
    probability=True,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE
).fit(X_svm_s, y_svm)

show(
    decision_surface(
        svm_linear,
        X_svm_s,
        y_svm,
        "Linear SVM probability surface"
    )
)

25. Kernel methods¶

A kernel evaluates an inner product in an implicit feature space:

$$ K(x,z)=\phi(x)^T\phi(z). $$

For the RBF kernel,

$$ K(x,z)= \exp(-\gamma\|x-z\|^2). $$

$\gamma$ controls locality.

  • small $\gamma$: broad, smooth influence;
  • large $\gamma$: highly local influence and more flexible boundaries.

The kernel trick allows nonlinear learning without explicitly constructing every transformed feature.

In [52]:
n_kernel = 550
X_kernel = rng.uniform(-2.5, 2.5, size=(n_kernel, 2))
radius = np.sqrt((X_kernel**2).sum(axis=1))
y_kernel = (radius > 1.35).astype(int)

flip = rng.random(n_kernel) < 0.05
y_kernel[flip] = 1-y_kernel[flip]

for gamma in [0.1, 1.0, 10.0]:
    model = SVC(
        kernel="rbf",
        C=2.0,
        gamma=gamma,
        probability=True,
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE
    ).fit(X_kernel, y_kernel)

    show(
        decision_surface(
            model,
            X_kernel,
            y_kernel,
            f"RBF SVM: gamma={gamma}"
        )
    )

26. Unifying model-complexity controls¶

Different algorithms expose different hyperparameters, but many are controlling the same latent quantity: effective flexibility.

Model Control Increasing it tends to...
Ridge $\lambda$ simplify
LASSO $\lambda$ simplify and sparsify
KNN $K$ smooth / simplify
Tree depth increase flexibility
SVM $C$ fit training points more aggressively
RBF SVM $\gamma$ make influence more local
Polynomial degree increase flexibility
Spline knots increase flexibility
Smoothing spline $\lambda$ smooth / simplify

The goal is always to balance:

$$ \text{approximation bias} \quad\text{against}\quad \text{estimation variance}. $$

27. End-to-end regression case study: Diabetes¶

We compare several model families on a real built-in dataset.

Models:

  • OLS;
  • Ridge;
  • LASSO;
  • KNN;
  • Decision Tree.

Metrics:

  • RMSE;
  • MAE;
  • $R^2$.

The purpose is not merely to choose the smallest RMSE.

We also compare assumptions, stability, interpretability, and likely failure modes.

In [53]:
diabetes = load_diabetes(as_frame=True)
df_d = diabetes.frame.copy()

X_d = df_d.drop(columns="target")
y_d = df_d["target"]

X_train_d, X_test_d, y_train_d, y_test_d = train_test_split(
    X_d, y_d,
    test_size=0.25,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE
)

reg_models = {
    "OLS": Pipeline([
        ("scale", StandardScaler()),
        ("model", LinearRegression())
    ]),
    "Ridge": Pipeline([
        ("scale", StandardScaler()),
        ("model", Ridge(alpha=10.0))
    ]),
    "LASSO": Pipeline([
        ("scale", StandardScaler()),
        ("model", Lasso(alpha=2.0, max_iter=20000))
    ]),
    "KNN": Pipeline([
        ("scale", StandardScaler()),
        ("model", KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=15))
    ]),
    "Decision Tree": DecisionTreeRegressor(
        max_depth=4,
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE
    )
}

rows = []
for name, model in reg_models.items():
    model.fit(X_train_d, y_train_d)
    pred = model.predict(X_test_d)
    m = Evaluator.regression(y_test_d, pred)
    rows.append({"model": name, **m.__dict__})

reg_benchmark = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("rmse").reset_index(drop=True)
show_df_table(reg_benchmark, "Diabetes regression benchmark")

    title="Regression benchmark: lower RMSE is better",
    width=880, height=440,
    x_range=reg_benchmark["model"].tolist(),
    x_axis_label="model",

Benchmarking caution¶

The models above use fixed hyperparameters for teaching clarity.

A rigorous comparison should tune every model on the training data only, preferably using cross-validation, and then evaluate the resulting chosen specifications on the same untouched test set.

Otherwise the comparison can favor models that happened to receive better hyperparameters.

28. End-to-end classification case study: Breast Cancer¶

We compare:

  • Logistic Regression;
  • KNN;
  • Decision Tree;
  • Linear SVM;
  • RBF SVM.

We report:

  • Accuracy;
  • Balanced Accuracy;
  • F1;
  • ROC AUC.

No single metric fully describes model behavior.

In [55]:
cancer = load_breast_cancer(as_frame=True)
X_c = cancer.data
y_c = (cancer.target == 0).astype(int)  # malignant = positive class

X_train_c, X_test_c, y_train_c, y_test_c = train_test_split(
    X_c, y_c,
    test_size=0.25,
    stratify=y_c,

)

}

rows = []
roc_curves = {}

for name, model in cls_models.items():
    model.fit(X_train_c, y_train_c)
    pred = model.predict(X_test_c)

cls_benchmark = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("roc_auc", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

29. ROC AUC interpretation¶

ROC compares

$$ TPR=\frac{TP}{TP+FN} $$

against

$$ FPR=\frac{FP}{FP+TN} $$

across thresholds.

ROC AUC primarily measures ranking ability.

It does not automatically tell us:

  • whether predicted probabilities are calibrated;
  • what deployment threshold should be used;
  • whether false positives are affordable;
  • whether false negatives are costly.

Metric selection should therefore follow the real decision problem.

30. Reusable cross-validation experiment runner¶

A modular evaluator reduces repetitive code and makes comparisons consistent.

This is particularly useful when experimenting with many model families.

In [57]:
@dataclass
class ClassificationExperimentRunner:
    models: Dict[str, object]
    cv: object

    def evaluate(self, X, y):
        scoring = {
            "accuracy": "accuracy",
            "balanced_accuracy": "balanced_accuracy",
            "f1": "f1",
            "roc_auc": "roc_auc"
        }

        rows = []
        for name, model in self.models.items():
            scores = cross_validate(
                clone(model),
                X, y,
                cv=self.cv,
                scoring=scoring,
                n_jobs=-1,
                return_train_score=False,
                error_score="raise"
            )

            rows.append({
                "model": name,
                "accuracy_mean": scores["test_accuracy"].mean(),
                "accuracy_sd": scores["test_accuracy"].std(ddof=1),
                "balanced_accuracy_mean": scores["test_balanced_accuracy"].mean(),
                "balanced_accuracy_sd": scores["test_balanced_accuracy"].std(ddof=1),
                "f1_mean": scores["test_f1"].mean(),
                "f1_sd": scores["test_f1"].std(ddof=1),
                "roc_auc_mean": scores["test_roc_auc"].mean(),
                "roc_auc_sd": scores["test_roc_auc"].std(ddof=1)
            })

        return (
            pd.DataFrame(rows)
            .sort_values("roc_auc_mean", ascending=False)
            .reset_index(drop=True)
        )
In [58]:
cv = StratifiedKFold(
    n_splits=5,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE
)

runner = ClassificationExperimentRunner(cls_models, cv)
cv_results = runner.evaluate(X_c, y_c)

show_df_table(cv_results, "5-fold classification cross-validation")

31. Computational complexity and engineering trade-offs¶

Model choice is not determined by predictive performance alone.

Approximate complexity intuition:

Method Broad computational behavior
OLS around $O(np^2+p^3)$ using normal-equation style algebra
Ridge similar algebra for one $\lambda$
Logistic regression iterative; full gradient around $O(np)$
LASSO iterative coordinate-descent style optimization
KNN training essentially storage
KNN prediction naively $O(np)$ per query
Tree fitting commonly around $O(np\log n)$ under favorable implementations
Kernel SVM potentially $O(n^2)$ memory and expensive optimization
Linear SVM substantially more scalable than kernel SVM

These are broad guides rather than universal implementation guarantees.

Real model selection may optimize:

$$ \boxed{ \text{accuracy} + \text{interpretability} + \text{latency} + \text{memory} + \text{training cost} + \text{stability}. } $$

32. The unifying optimization view¶

Many algorithms can be written as

$$ \boxed{ \hat f = \arg\min_f \left[ \text{data-fit loss} + \lambda\,\text{complexity penalty} \right]. } $$

OLS¶

$$ \min_\beta \sum_i(y_i-x_i^T\beta)^2 $$

Ridge¶

$$ \min_\beta \sum_i(y_i-x_i^T\beta)^2 + \lambda\|\beta\|_2^2 $$

LASSO¶

$$ \min_\beta \sum_i(y_i-x_i^T\beta)^2 + \lambda\|\beta\|_1 $$

Logistic regression¶

$$ \min_\beta-\ell(\beta) $$

SVM¶

$$ \min_w \sum_i\max(0,1-y_if(x_i)) + \lambda\|w\|_2^2 $$

Smoothing spline¶

$$ \min_f \sum_i(y_i-f(x_i))^2 + \lambda\int[f''(x)]^2dx. $$

The algorithms differ in the function class, loss and penalty, but the statistical structure is remarkably similar.

33. A methodical ST5227 problem-solving workflow¶

When faced with a new dataset, ask:

Step 1 — What is the response type?¶

  • continuous?
  • binary?
  • count?
  • multiclass?

Step 2 — What assumptions are plausible?¶

  • linear relationship?
  • constant variance?
  • sparse signal?
  • nonlinear boundary?
  • local smoothness?

Step 3 — What loss or likelihood matches the problem?¶

Step 4 — What hypothesis class is appropriate?¶

  • linear;
  • polynomial;
  • spline;
  • local learner;
  • tree;
  • kernel.

Step 5 — What controls flexibility?¶

  • $\lambda$;
  • $K$;
  • depth;
  • $C$;
  • $\gamma$;
  • number of knots.

Step 6 — What happens to bias and variance?¶

Step 7 — How will hyperparameters be selected?¶

Use validation or cross-validation.

Step 8 — What metric reflects the actual decision cost?¶

Step 9 — Is the final solution stable, interpretable and computationally practical?¶

This reasoning process is more transferable than memorizing API calls.

34. Student exercises¶

Exercise 1 — Multicollinearity¶

Repeat the multicollinearity simulation using perturbation scales:

$$ 0.3,\quad0.1,\quad0.01,\quad0.001. $$

Track:

  • condition number;
  • OLS coefficients;
  • Ridge coefficients.

Explain the pattern.

Exercise 2 — LASSO support recovery¶

Vary:

  • sample size;
  • number of irrelevant predictors;
  • noise.

When does LASSO recover the sparse signal well?

Exercise 3 — Cross-validation uncertainty¶

Repeat Ridge cross-validation using multiple random seeds.

Does the selected $\alpha$ remain identical?

What does this reveal about model-selection uncertainty?

Exercise 4 — Classification threshold¶

For the cancer classifier, find thresholds that:

  • minimize false negatives;
  • maximize F1;
  • achieve sensitivity above 95%.

Compare false-positive rates.

Exercise 5 — Splines¶

Try:

$$ 3,\ 5,\ 8,\ 12,\ 20 $$

knots.

Compute training and test RMSE.

Can you observe the familiar bias–variance pattern?

Exercise 6 — Curse of dimensionality¶

Generate problems with:

$$ p=2,\ 10,\ 50,\ 100,\ 500. $$

Compare KNN with regularized logistic regression.

Why does KNN usually deteriorate more rapidly?

35. Suggested second notebook¶

A natural continuation would extend the framework to:

  • subset selection and information criteria;
  • bootstrap;
  • discriminant analysis;
  • generalized additive models;
  • local polynomial regression;
  • kernel regression;
  • bagging;
  • Random Forests;
  • boosting and gradient boosting;
  • nested cross-validation;
  • calibration;
  • feature importance;
  • partial dependence;
  • SHAP;
  • high-dimensional asymptotics.

All of these continue the same conceptual chain:

$$ \boxed{ \text{loss} \rightarrow \text{estimation} \rightarrow \text{regularization} \rightarrow \text{complexity} \rightarrow \text{generalization}. } $$

36. Final summary¶

The key statistical-learning workflow is:

$$ \boxed{ \text{Data} \rightarrow \text{Model class} \rightarrow \text{Loss / likelihood} \rightarrow \text{Optimization} \rightarrow \text{Estimator} \rightarrow \text{Bias + variance} \rightarrow \text{Validation} \rightarrow \text{Generalization}. } $$

OLS, Ridge, LASSO, GLMs, splines, KNN, trees and SVMs are not isolated algorithms.

They are different solutions to the same broader problem:

How can we extract repeatable signal from finite noisy data while controlling model complexity strongly enough to generalize?

That is the central mindset this notebook is designed to build.
